channel.title: Agentic on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Agentic on Best of AI

item.title: 11x
item.description:
11x’s pitch is that AI can do the work of a sales development representative. Alice researches prospects, writes personalized outreach, sends messages across email and LinkedIn, and tries to book meetings. A voice agent, Julian, makes phone calls and follows up. The company presents them as digital workers that run around the clock.

Customers connect their CRM and define the audience and message guidelines, and the agents work through lead lists and hand interested prospects to human salespeople. The approach can raise the volume of outreach well beyond what a small team could do by hand, though response quality depends on targeting and data.

item.title: Azure AI Foundry
item.description: Foundry is where Microsoft brings together its AI development tools for businesses. A catalog lists models from OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, and others, which you can test side by side and deploy through one set of APIs. Everything runs under Azure’s identity, networking, and compliance controls, which is what many regulated companies need before they can use generative AI. The service has gone through several names, including Azure AI Studio, so older tutorials may use different labels.

item.title: BabyAGI
item.description:
BabyAGI arrived early in the wave of autonomous agent experiments. The original script was only a few dozen lines: given an objective, a language model creates a task list, executes the first task, stores the result in a vector database, then generates and reprioritizes new tasks based on what it learned. That simple loop was widely copied and adapted.

The project mattered because it made the idea of an AI agent easy to understand and try. It sparked many descendants and discussion about what autonomous systems could do, and developers learned from its limits, such as loops, drift, and cost. Later versions were reworked into a framework for building self-improving agents with functions stored in a database.

item.title: LangGraph
item.description:
LangGraph models an agent as a graph. Each node is a step, such as calling a model, running a tool, or checking a condition, and edges define the flow between steps, including loops and branches. A shared state object passes information along. This explicit structure gives developers control over what the agent does and when, which makes complex agents easier to reason about than a free-running loop.

Features aimed at production use set it apart. Checkpointing saves state so a run can pause and resume, or recover from failure. Human-in-the-loop steps let an agent wait for approval before taking an action, and time-travel debugging lets developers replay and edit earlier steps. It supports streaming of intermediate results, long-term memory, and multi-agent designs, in Python and JavaScript.

item.title: Microsoft Copilot Studio
item.description:
Copilot Studio lets organizations create their own AI agents without heavy coding. In a visual editor, makers describe an agent’s purpose, connect knowledge sources such as SharePoint sites and websites, add topics and actions, and test it in a chat window. The finished agent can be published to Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, websites, and messaging channels, and can answer questions, complete tasks, or hand off to people.

Its strength is connection to business systems. Hundreds of connectors reach tools like Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP, and Dynamics 365, and agents can use Power Automate flows to run processes. Autonomous agents can respond to triggers such as a new email or record, not only a chat message, and the platform supports the Model Context Protocol to reach more tools. Administrators manage governance, data loss prevention, and access through Microsoft’s admin centers.

item.title: SuperAGI
item.description:
SuperAGI appeared during the first wave of autonomous agent interest. It offered a framework and dashboard for creating agents that use tools, with features for running several agents at once, managing resources, and viewing performance.

The company later built applications on top of the framework for sales and marketing automation. Many agent frameworks have emerged since, and the field has moved toward different designs and commercial platforms.

SuperAGI is open source, with paid products. Check its repository for current activity. Alternatives include LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, OpenAI Agents SDK, and Dify. SuperAGI suits developers who want to explore an open agent platform.

item.title: Beam
item.description: Beam is Reflection’s open sparse mixture-of-experts model, with 501B total and 23B active parameters under Apache 2.0. It is built for coding, reasoning, and agentic work.

item.title: Gemini 4 Carbon
item.description: Gemini 4 Carbon targets cybersecurity defense and long-horizon tasks. Google rolled it out on October 28, 2026, to a limited group through the Fairwind Program.

item.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro
item.description: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 23, 2026. It is a 3T-class model with a 1M-token context window, aimed at coding, 3D, financial research, and agentic tasks. A faster Highspeed variant launched the same day.

item.title: Ling-3.1-flash
item.description: Ling-3.1-flash is a hybrid reasoning model from InclusionAI with 560B total and about 25B active parameters and a 1M-token context. It targets agent, search, office, and coding tasks.

item.title: Mellum2.1
item.description: JetBrains released Mellum2.1 on October 8, 2026, an open 12B mixture-of-experts model for coding agents. It was trained with reinforcement learning in coding environments.

item.title: Muse Spark Open
item.description: Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta, with 816B total and 42B active parameters and a 1M-token context window. It targets coding and agentic work.

item.title: Muse Wonder
item.description: Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are agent models that use Active Memory and Active Focus for long tasks. They are available through the Meta Model API and Muse Code.

item.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL
item.description: NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and a 74B-A9B Bolt variant on October 15, 2026, for multimodal agent workflows.

item.title: Kimi Code
item.description:
Kimi Code is a command line agent in the same family as Claude Code and Codex CLI. You start it in a project folder, describe a task, and it reads files, edits code, runs commands, and checks results, deciding what to do next based on what happens. Permissions let you approve risky actions.

It defaults to Moonshot AI’s Kimi models, which are known for strong coding and long context, and can also connect to other compatible providers. Features include built-in subagents for coding, exploring, and planning, support for the Model Context Protocol to connect tools, lifecycle hooks for automation and safety checks, and an ACP mode so editors like Zed and JetBrains can drive it.

item.title: Claude Duet
item.description: Duet is built on the idea that an assistant should not wait for you to ask. Each morning it sends a brief on what matters across your connected apps, and it checks those accounts every few hours for new items that need attention. You can hand it tasks, and it works on its own virtual machine with a browser, so your laptop or phone does not need to stay on. It keeps working while you are away and tells you when something is done or needs a decision.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5
item.description: Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 on September 28, 2026, a week after Claude Opus 5.5. Anthropic says it generates output more than 30% faster than Claude Sonnet 5 while keeping the same API pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached-input reads at $0.20. The context window stays at 1 million tokens.

item.title: GPT-6 Sol
item.description: OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol on September 22, 2026, alongside the cheaper GPT-6 Luna, positioning both below the earlier GPT-6 Astra flagship in the GPT-6 lineup. Sol reads up to 1.05 million tokens of context and writes up to 128,000 tokens of output, aimed at coding and agentic tasks rather than Astra’s recurrent-depth reasoning. API pricing runs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with a $0.20 rate for cached input.

item.title: MiniMax M3.1-Flash-Preview
item.description: MiniMax released M3.1-Flash-Preview on September 27, 2026, its first model under the M3.1 name. It reads up to 1 million tokens of context but only runs inside MiniMax’s own coding tool, MiniMax Code, rather than through a general API. MiniMax has not published pricing, throughput, or benchmark numbers for it yet.

item.title: Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash
item.description: Alibaba released Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash in late September 2026 as a single model that accepts text, image, audio, and video input and responds in text, built for agentic and multimodal workloads. It carries a 1 million token context window and is available through Alibaba Cloud and as open weights on Hugging Face.

item.title: OpenAI Dots
item.description: Dots move ChatGPT from a tool you open to an assistant that keeps working. Each dot has its own cloud computer with a browser, so it can carry out tasks on websites and in apps without tying up your device. You give it goals, such as keeping track of your inbox, preparing for meetings, or monitoring a project, and it works in the background, checking back when it needs input. Over time it learns from your feedback.

item.title: Atria Dawn Preview
item.description:
Shanghai AI Laboratory released Atria Dawn Preview on September 11, 2026, an open-weight preview built on a 744-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts foundation and aimed squarely at agentic research and engineering work rather than chat. The design goal is a full loop (problem analysis, tool use, code implementation, running experiments, reading the results, and recovering from failures) rather than answering a question and stopping.

The lab shipped it under an MIT license alongside a 143-author paper studying how the model performed during its own development: across 769 recorded tasks from 56 participants, roughly a third were rated by the humans involved as infeasible without AI assistance.

item.title: Gemini 3.8 Flash
item.description:
Google pushed out Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2, 2026, keeping the same 1,048,576 token context window and 65,536 token output ceiling as 3.7 Flash while posting solid gains on software engineering, agentic, and multi-step reasoning benchmarks. Introductory pricing holds at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens through the end of 2026, after which it doubles to $1.50 and $7.50.

Alongside it, Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, a locked-down variant tuned for vulnerability discovery and patching, available only to vetted defenders through the new Fairwind Program rather than the general API.

item.title: Grok Bot
item.description:
Grok Bot takes a different shape from a chat window. A user creates named bots and assigns them tasks, and each bot runs in the cloud, keeps working after the user closes their laptop, and can sign into apps and use a browser to complete work. Examples include handling inbox tasks, researching topics, and running routine workflows.

The product emphasizes persistence. Bots remember context over time and report back, and the cloud computer gives them a place to store files and run tools. It is positioned for both individuals and businesses, with a business version aimed at agents that log into company applications.

item.title: Hy4 Preview
item.description:
Tencent open-sourced Hy4 Preview on August 28, 2026, a 770-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 49 billion active parameters and a 1 million token context window, released under Apache 2.0. Rather than building a general chat model, Tencent’s Hunyuan team trained it on work data from software engineers, game developers, finance analysts, and security experts, and co-designed it alongside the company’s own CodeBuddy and WorkBuddy products.

In Tencent’s internal blind evaluation, where 163 experts judged 203 real engineering tasks, Hy4 Preview averaged 2.99 out of 4.00, edging out GLM-5.3 at 2.92 and Kimi K3 at 2.94. API pricing runs $0.834 per million input tokens and $2.501 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.042 per million.

item.title: Kimi K2.8 Preview
item.description: Moonshot AI rolled out Kimi K2.8 Preview on September 11, 2026, slotting it between the open-weight Kimi K2.7 Code and flagship Kimi K3. It landed inside Kimi Code and Kimi Work the same day with no configuration changes needed, added image and video input on top of text, and bumped every membership tier’s context window from 262,144 to 1 million tokens. Adjustable thinking effort (low, high, or max) now matches the K3 series, with max as the default.

item.title: Sider Omni Sidebar
item.description:
Sider began as a browser sidebar for chatting with AI about web pages. Omni Sidebar extends the idea to the whole Mac: a panel that sees the content in the active app and lets users ask questions, summarize, draft replies, or take actions without copying and pasting.

The assistant supports several underlying models and can work with files and screenshots. For people who live in email, documents, and spreadsheets, an assistant that sees the same screen saves steps.

item.title: Meta Muse
item.description: Muse is Meta’s step from a chat assistant to an agent that acts on your behalf. You ask it to do something, such as arrange a trip, draft and send an email, or handle a multi-step errand, and it works across apps and websites to complete the job. Each user’s agent runs in a secure virtual machine, so it can continue working after you leave the app and come back when it needs a decision.

item.title: Muse Glimmer
item.description: Meta released Muse Glimmer on August 10, 2026, a 30 billion parameter model distilled from its larger Muse Spark 1.2 and built specifically to run always-on agentic tasks on a single consumer GPU rather than in the cloud. It pairs a causal language model with a dedicated perception encoder, folding multi-step reasoning, tool use, multimodal understanding, and failure recovery into one model that keeps working without network access. Meta says it beats similarly sized models from Google and Alibaba on agentic benchmarks and holds its own against models twice its size on reasoning tasks. Weights are open under the Apache 2.0 license, aimed at developers building privacy-sensitive coding assistants, document analysis tools, and personal agents that need to run locally.

item.title: Muse Spark 1.3
item.description: Meta shipped Muse Spark 1.3 on September 2, 2026, its biggest coding and agentic jump yet and, according to AI chief Alexandr Wang, a model that closes much of the gap with frontier releases like GPT-5.6. It cuts token usage by 25 percent and tool calls by 20 percent on comparable tasks, and holds the same $1.25 per million input and $4.25 per million output token pricing as its predecessor, plus a contributor tier at a steep discount for developers who let Meta train on their prompts and completions. Access starts through Muse Code and the Meta API, with a “max reasoning” variant still going through safety testing before release, and a rollout to Meta AI, Instagram, and Facebook planned to follow.

item.title: MagiCrew
item.description:
MagiCrew packages agent capabilities in one open-source system. A general agent can plan and complete tasks with tools, a visual workflow editor lets users build repeatable processes, and messaging and collaboration features let teams work with agents in shared spaces.

Because it is open source, organizations can host it themselves and adapt it, which appeals to teams with privacy requirements or specific needs. It extends an existing open-source project, which gives it a base of users and code to build on.

item.title: ChatGPT Atlas
item.description:
Atlas puts ChatGPT inside the browser. A sidebar assistant can see the page you are on, so you can ask it to summarize an article, explain a table, compare products across tabs, or draft a reply in context. The address bar can also act as a chat prompt, and the browser can remember context from your browsing if you turn that on.

Agent mode goes further. The assistant can take actions on your behalf, such as navigating to a site, filling in a form, or doing research across several pages, while you watch and can take over. This capability is powerful and also risky, since web pages can contain instructions meant to trick an agent, a problem known as prompt injection.

item.title: GLM-5.2 Turbo
item.description: Zhipu AI released GLM-5.2 Turbo on August 17, 2026 as a faster sibling to GLM-5.2, built specifically for agent-driven workloads rather than general chat or one-off queries. It carries a smaller context window than the base model, about 200,000 tokens versus GLM-5.2’s full 1-million-token capacity, in exchange for lower latency on the long execution chains typical of coding agents and automation tools. Zhipu says it improved complex instruction decomposition and tool use, along with stability across scheduled and persistent tasks that run for extended periods without human supervision.

item.title: GLM-5.3-Flash
item.description: Zhipu AI officially revealed GLM-5.3-Flash on August 26, 2026, confirming it as the model previously seeded anonymously on testing platforms under the name “Ox Alpha,” which had drawn over 50 trillion tokens of traffic in five days before anyone knew who built it. It’s a 320-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 18 billion active parameters per token, the first natively multimodal release in the GLM-5 line, combining a hybrid sparse-and-linear attention design with a 1-million-token context window. Zhipu pretrained it on a 30-trillion-token multimodal corpus and says it matches Nvidia GPU-based models on efficiency and token cost while running on domestic Chinese chips.

item.title: Grok 4.6
item.description: xAI released Grok 4.6 on August 12, 2026, extending Grok 4.5’s coding focus toward longer-running agent sessions and more demanding interactive and visual tasks. The model carries a 500,000-token context window, accepts text and image input, and exposes configurable reasoning effort levels from low to xhigh so developers can trade off latency against depth on a given request. xAI priced it at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens for prompts under 200,000 tokens, with rates roughly doubling once a request crosses that threshold.

item.title: Viktor
item.description:
Viktor lives where teams already talk. Instead of a separate app, a colleague mentions Viktor in a channel and asks for something, such as pulling numbers from a dashboard, building a report, or writing a script, and it replies in the thread. It watches how the team works and picks up context over time.

It connects to a very large number of business tools, so it can read from and act in systems like CRMs, analytics, and ad platforms, and it can produce artifacts such as documents and simple web apps. Skills can be added for specialized work.

item.title: Gemini 3.7 Flash
item.description: Google shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash on August 13, 2026, just three weeks after 3.6 Flash, keeping the same 1,048,576 token input window and 65,536 token output ceiling while moving the knowledge cutoff to March 2026. Google credits the gains to developer feedback and algorithmic changes rather than a bigger model, and the benchmark jumps are large: DeepSWE v1.1 climbs from 49.0 to 65.3 percent, FrontierCode 1.1 Main goes from 34.4 to 43.6 percent, and Zapier’s AutomationBench nearly doubles from 17.0 to 30.4 percent. Input pricing is cut in half to $0.75 per million tokens as introductory pricing through the end of 2026.

item.title: GLM-5.3
item.description: Zhipu AI released GLM-5.3 on August 14, 2026, calling it the strongest open-weights coding model available, though the weights themselves are not landing until two weeks after the announcement. It shares its base architecture with GLM-5.2, so the roughly 50 percent jump in coding capability Zhipu reports comes entirely from extended post-training rather than a larger model. The company points to a security angle in particular: GLM-5.3 scored 84.5 percent on CyberGym, a benchmark for finding and validating vulnerabilities from source code, edging out Anthropic’s Claude Mythos at 83.8 percent and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol at 83.6 percent. Zhipu says internal security teams used the model to surface 2,436 vulnerabilities across 269 projects.

item.title: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731
item.description: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 moves DeepSeek-V4-Flash out of preview and into public beta as a re-post-trained checkpoint, announced July 31, 2026 in the company’s API changelog. The architecture is unchanged from the model’s April debut, a 284 billion parameter mixture-of-experts design with 13 billion active parameters per token, a shared expert plus 256 routed experts, and a 1 million token context window. What changed is the post-training pipeline: DeepSeek retuned it specifically for coding, agentic tool use, and reasoning, and the API now natively supports the Responses format and works with Codex out of the box. It remains MIT-licensed and ungated, so teams can self-host it commercially without restriction, with roughly 110 GB of memory needed at 3-bit quantization or a 4x GB300 node for full precision. API pricing stayed low at $0.14 per million input tokens and $0.28 per million output tokens.

item.title: Ling-3.0-Flash
item.description: Ling-3.0-Flash is the latest entry in Ant Group’s efficiency-focused Ling line, built by its inclusionAI lab and unveiled July 23, 2026 as a hybrid-reasoning foundation model for production AI agent workloads. It’s a 124 billion parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates only about 5.1 billion parameters per token, natively supports a 256,000 token context window that can scale up to 1 million, and Ant says it matches or beats models two to three times its parameter count on reasoning, instruction following, and long-context benchmarks. A cluster-level hierarchical caching system cuts time-to-first-token on long conversations by 60 to 80 percent. Ant priced the first-party API at $0.075 per million input tokens and $0.22 per million output tokens, among the cheapest rates measured for a model scoring 38 or above on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, and released the weights on Hugging Face under the MIT license.

item.title: Muse Spark 1.2
item.description: Muse Spark 1.2 is a coding-focused point release of Muse Spark 1.1 rather than a new base model, shipped August 5, 2026 alongside Muse Code, Meta’s first terminal coding agent. It keeps the 1,048,576 token context window and roughly 131,072 max output tokens from 1.1, and was co-trained with the new agent using rejection-sampled harness trajectories plus a self-improvement loop. Meta reports a jump from 76.2 to 82.9 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and from 53.0 to 59.3 percent on DeepSWE v1.1 over the previous version. Standard API pricing holds at $1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 per million output tokens, and Meta added a separate contributor tier at $0.10 input and $0.20 output in exchange for permission to train future models on submitted prompts and completions.

item.title: Poolside Laguna S 2.1
item.description: Laguna S 2.1, released July 21, 2026, is Poolside’s open-weight foundation model for agentic coding, a 118 billion parameter mixture-of-experts system that activates 8 billion parameters per token and supports up to a 1,048,576 token context window. It scores 78.5 percent on SWE-Bench Multilingual, tops the published table among open models of disclosed size, and reaches 70.2 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1 while staying competitive with rivals many times larger. Weights are available on Hugging Face under Poolside’s own OpenMDW-1.1 license, and hosted access through OpenRouter runs free up to a 256K context window, with the full 1 million token context priced at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.20 per million output tokens.

item.title: Comet
item.description:
Comet makes the assistant part of the browser. Instead of copying content into a chatbot, users can ask questions about the page they are on, compare information across tabs, summarize a thread, or have the assistant search and collect results. Perplexity’s answer engine is the default way to search.

An agent mode lets the assistant take actions, such as filling in forms, managing a calendar or inbox, or completing a purchase flow, while the user watches and can step in. This gives it the power and the risks of any browsing agent, including exposure to prompt injection from malicious web pages.

item.title: Genspark
item.description:
Genspark started as an AI search engine and expanded into an agent workspace. A user states a goal, such as researching a market and building a presentation, and the Super Agent plans the steps, searches the web, uses tools, and produces outputs like slide decks, documents, spreadsheets, and media.

It combines several models and tools behind the scenes, and offers specialized agents for tasks like calling businesses on a user’s behalf, creating images and video, and building simple websites. Results appear in a workspace where users can review and edit them.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.6
item.description: Claude Opus 4.6, released February 5, 2026, expanded the Opus line’s context window to 1 million tokens, up from the 200,000 tokens Opus 4.5 shipped with three months earlier. Anthropic held pricing steady at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens and focused the update on coding: the model plans more carefully before writing code, sustains agentic tasks over longer sessions, and catches more of its own mistakes during code review. It’s available across claude.ai, the Claude API, and the major cloud platforms, and it became the base Anthropic built the Sonnet 4.6 release on two weeks later.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 4.6
item.description: Claude Sonnet 4.6 shipped on February 17, 2026 and became the default model in claude.ai and Claude Cowork, Anthropic’s workspace product. It matches Opus 4.6’s 1 million token context window and 128,000 token output limit while pricing in at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, roughly a fifth of Opus 4.6’s rate. On SWE-bench Verified it scored 79.6 percent, within a few points of the Opus model despite the price gap, and it posted 59.1 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 72.5 percent on OSWorld-Verified, benchmarks that test agentic terminal and computer-use tasks. Anthropic built in extended reasoning chains that can run up to 100 steps, aimed at developers who want Opus-level reliability without paying Opus prices.

item.title: GPT-5.4
item.description: GPT-5.4, released March 5, 2026, was the first general-purpose OpenAI model to ship with native computer-use capability, reaching 75 percent on the OSWorld benchmark for controlling a desktop environment directly. It expanded the context window to roughly 1 million tokens (922,000 input plus 128,000 output), added a five-level reasoning effort control, and introduced a tool-search mechanism that OpenAI says cuts token costs by 47 percent in workflows that call a lot of external tools. Standard API pricing is $2.50 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with a GPT-5.4 Pro tier at $30/$180 for maximum accuracy. OpenAI followed up on March 17 with GPT-5.4 Mini, priced at $0.75/$4.50 and available to free ChatGPT users, plus a developer-only GPT-5.4 Nano tier.

item.title: Kimi K2.5
item.description: Kimi K2.5 is Moonshot AI’s native multimodal update to Kimi K2, released January 27, 2026 after continued pretraining over roughly 15 trillion mixed text and image tokens on top of the original K2 base. It’s built around what Moonshot calls Agent Swarm, letting the model coordinate up to 100 specialized sub-agents working on a task at once, and it pairs strong visual coding ability with the agentic tool-calling focus of earlier Kimi releases. The model carries a 262,144 token context window with up to 98,000 tokens of output, and Moonshot’s own API prices it around $0.44 per million input tokens and $2.00 per million output tokens, with third-party providers pricing it similarly. Like the rest of the Kimi K2 line, it ships with open weights under a modified MIT license, and it sat between the original K2 and the later K2.6 and K2.7 Code releases.

item.title: MiniMax M2.5
item.description: MiniMax M2.5, released February 12, 2026, extends the coding-focused M2.1 model into general office work: generating and editing Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files and switching between different software environments within an agentic workflow. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 230 billion total parameters and 10 billion active per token, ships with a 204,800 token context window and up to 128,000 tokens of output, and comes in two variants, a standard mode running at roughly 50 tokens per second and a Lightning mode at double that speed. MiniMax prices API access at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.90 per million output tokens, among the cheapest rates of any frontier-class model at release, and it ships with open weights under a modified MIT license for self-hosting.

item.title: OpenAI Presence
item.description:
Presence aims to let companies put OpenAI-powered agents on the front line of conversations. Businesses configure agents that talk with customers by phone or chat and handle employee requests, connecting them to company systems so they can look up information and take actions.

The platform combines the models with enterprise features: tools for building and testing agents, integrations, monitoring, and controls to keep agents within policy. It competes with specialized customer service AI vendors and with platforms from other model providers.

item.title: Baidu Qianfan
item.description:
Qianfan is Baidu’s cloud platform for building with large models. Companies can call Baidu’s ERNIE models and a selection of third-party and open models through a common API, then build applications such as chatbots, search over internal documents, and automated workflows. The platform covers the steps in between, including prompt engineering, fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment.

It includes tools for agents and retrieval, with knowledge-base features that let applications answer from a company’s own data, plus plugins and workflows for connecting to business systems. Qianfan is used heavily within China, where Baidu offers local hosting and compliance with domestic regulations.

item.title: Cohere North
item.description:
North is Cohere’s platform for putting agents to work inside companies. Employees use a chat interface and can build agents without code for tasks in HR, finance, IT, and other areas, connecting them to the apps and documents they already use. Search across company data is powered by Cohere’s own retrieval technology.

Security and control are the main pitch. Organizations can deploy North in a private cloud, on premises, or in air-gapped settings, which appeals to banks, governments, and defense contractors with strict data rules. Cohere designs the models for enterprise use and works with customers on custom solutions.

item.title: Palantir AIP
item.description:
AIP, the Artificial Intelligence Platform, is Palantir’s layer for putting language models to work on an organization’s data. It builds on Palantir’s ontology, a structured model of a company’s objects, such as orders, machines, and customers, and the actions that can be taken on them. Models can then read and act within that governed model instead of working on raw text.

Customers build agents and applications that automate tasks, answer questions, and support decisions in areas like supply chain, healthcare, defense, and manufacturing. Controls around access, logging, and human approval aim to make AI usable in sensitive settings. Palantir runs engagement programs that help customers reach production quickly.

item.title: Tencent Cloud ADP
item.description:
Tencent Cloud ADP gives companies tools to create agents. Users connect knowledge bases for retrieval, design workflows with a visual editor, and combine agents that work together. Models include Tencent’s Hunyuan family and others.

Typical applications are customer service, internal assistants, and process automation. The platform includes tools for testing and monitoring and integrates with Tencent’s ecosystem, including WeChat and enterprise messaging.

It is sold on usage-based pricing within Tencent Cloud. Outside China, availability and support are more limited, and organizations must consider data residency. Alternatives include Alibaba Cloud’s Bailian, Baidu Qianfan, ByteDance’s Volcano Engine, Dify, and AWS Bedrock Agents. Tencent Cloud ADP suits companies building agents on Tencent Cloud.

item.title: Claude Opus 4
item.description: Claude Opus 4 launched on May 22, 2025 as Anthropic’s flagship model, released alongside the smaller Claude Sonnet 4. It was built for sustained, long-horizon agentic work such as multi-hour coding sessions and research tasks that involve using tools repeatedly across a long thread, rather than answering a single prompt. Anthropic reported it leading on SWE-bench Verified at launch, at roughly 72.5 percent, and it can use tools, including web search, during extended thinking and run several tools in parallel. It runs on a 200,000 token context window, reads images as well as text, and is priced at $15 per million input tokens and $75 per million output tokens, the same rate Anthropic had charged for Claude 3 Opus a year earlier.

item.title: Claude Opus 4.1
item.description: Claude Opus 4.1, released in August 2025, is a targeted update to Claude Opus 4 rather than a new generation. Anthropic focused the update on coding and agentic accuracy, and it pushed the SWE-bench Verified score up to roughly 74.5 percent, a meaningful jump on the real-world GitHub issue benchmark that Anthropic uses to track coding ability. It kept the same 200,000 token context window, image input support, and $15/$75 per million token pricing as Opus 4, and it gained the ability to use up to 64,000 tokens of extended thinking for harder problems. Anthropic described it as a drop-in replacement for Opus 4, meant to hold the top of the Opus line until the next full model generation shipped.

item.title: Claude Sonnet 4.5
item.description: Claude Sonnet 4.5, released on September 29, 2025, was Anthropic’s highest-scoring Sonnet-tier model on SWE-bench Verified at launch, reaching about 77.2 percent on the full 500-problem set with extended thinking enabled. Anthropic built it heavily around coding and computer use, and testers reported it staying focused on a single complex task for more than 30 hours without losing track of what it was doing. It added context awareness, meaning the model tracks how much of its context window remains during a long conversation and adjusts its behavior as it fills up, which matters for agents running long unattended sessions. It kept Sonnet’s $3/$15 per million token pricing and 200,000 token standard context window, with a 1 million token context window available in beta, making it Anthropic’s primary recommendation for coding agents and long-running automation through the rest of 2025.

item.title: Devstral
item.description: Devstral is a 24-billion-parameter code model that Mistral AI released on May 21, 2025, built in collaboration with All Hands AI, the team behind the OpenHands agent framework. Unlike most code models, which are tuned mainly for autocomplete or single-turn code generation, Devstral is trained specifically for agentic coding: exploring a codebase across multiple files, using tools, and completing multi-step software engineering tasks. On SWE-bench Verified it scored 46.8%, ahead of every open model available at release and even some larger proprietary ones.

item.title: Fuyu-8B
item.description: Fuyu-8B is a multimodal model Adept AI released in October 2023, built specifically to support digital agents that need to see and act on screens rather than to serve as a general-purpose chatbot. Adept designed it around a simplified architecture: it feeds image patches directly into a standard decoder-only transformer without a separate image encoder, which lets it accept images at whatever resolution they come in instead of resizing everything to a fixed size. That matters for Adept’s use case, since it needs to read UI elements, buttons, and text at native resolution to answer questions about screenshots, graphs, and diagrams, and to localize specific elements on a screen. Adept released the 8 billion parameter model on Hugging Face under a CC-BY-NC license, meaning it’s free to use and modify but not for commercial purposes, positioning it as a smaller public preview of the model that powers Adept’s own product rather than a fully separate offering. It supports a 16K token context window, and Adept has since been acquired, with much of its team moving to Amazon in 2024, leaving Fuyu-8B as a snapshot of its agent-focused research direction.

item.title: Kimi K2.6
item.description: Kimi K2.6 is Moonshot AI’s open-weight flagship model, released in April 2026 as the successor to the original Kimi K2. It is a 1-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates about 32 billion parameters per token, ships natively in INT4 for cheaper inference, and handles a 262,144-token context window. The model is built for long-running agentic work: Moonshot designed it around multi-agent orchestration, coding sessions that run for hours without human intervention, and native multimodal input rather than bolted-on vision. Independent evaluations from Artificial Analysis rank it as the strongest open-weight model available, putting it within a few points of closed frontier systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on tasks like SWE-Bench Pro and Humanity’s Last Exam, while charging a fraction of their per-token price. Moonshot releases the weights under a modified MIT license, so anyone can download and self-host the model rather than relying on Moonshot’s own API.

item.title: Kimi K2.7 Code
item.description: Kimi K2.7 Code is Moonshot AI’s coding-focused model, released in June 2026 as a specialized build on top of Kimi K2.6. It keeps the same 1-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts architecture with about 32 billion active parameters and a 256,000-token context window, but tunes the model specifically for long-horizon coding and agentic task decomposition. Moonshot reports gains of roughly 22% on its Kimi Code Bench v2, 11% on Program Bench, and 31.5% on MLS Bench Lite over K2.6, along with about 30% fewer reasoning tokens spent per task, which lowers the effective cost of running it in an agent loop. The model always runs in thinking mode and does not support a non-thinking fallback, and it accepts text, image, and video input alongside code. Weights are open on Hugging Face, and Moonshot’s own API prices it well below closed competitors like Claude Opus and GPT-5.5 on both input and output tokens.

item.title: ChatGPT Work
item.description: ChatGPT Work extends ChatGPT from answering questions to doing jobs. You describe an outcome, such as preparing a weekly status report, building a slide deck from a folder of notes, or reconciling figures between two spreadsheets, and the agent works through it step by step. It gathers context from connected tools, uses a browser and code when needed, and produces finished files. Tasks can run for a long time without you watching, and you can return to review the result.

item.title: Letta
item.description:
Letta grew out of the MemGPT research project, which proposed managing an agent’s memory like an operating system manages memory. In Letta, an agent has a core memory it always sees and external stores it can read and write, so it can keep information across conversations that far exceed a model’s context window.

Developers create agents through an API, define their tools and memory blocks, and let them run over long periods. This suits assistants that need to remember user preferences, companions, and agents that learn from experience. A hosted platform manages deployment, and tools let developers inspect and edit what an agent remembers.

item.title: Lindy
item.description:
Lindy lets people create agents without code. A user describes a task or chooses a template, connects apps like Gmail, Slack, and a CRM, and defines triggers and steps. The Lindy then runs on its own: sorting an inbox, drafting replies, booking meetings, or updating records.

Workflows can include several steps with conditions, and Lindies can hand tasks to each other or ask a human for approval. A phone agent product handles calls, and a large catalog of integrations connects to business tools.

item.title: Stack AI
item.description:
Stack AI offers a visual builder for AI workflows. Users drag together components such as inputs, language models, document search, and outputs, then connect them to enterprise tools. The result can be deployed as a chatbot, form, or API.

Common cases include document processing, internal knowledge assistants, and support triage. The platform emphasizes security and governance, with options for private deployment. Templates give a starting point.

Stack AI has a free tier and paid plans. Workflows need testing and monitoring. Alternatives include Relevance AI, Dify, Flowise, n8n, and Microsoft Copilot Studio. Stack AI suits business teams building AI workflows without code.

item.title: Agent GPT
item.description: AgentGPT was one of the first tools that made autonomous agents easy to try. You open a web page, name an agent, describe a goal like planning a trip or researching a market, and click deploy. The agent then writes its own list of tasks, executes them one by one using a language model, and revises the list as it learns. Watching it reason through a goal in real time was a vivid demonstration of the idea behind agents.

item.title: Agno
item.description:
Agno, formerly called Phidata, aims to make agent building straightforward and fast. A developer defines an agent in a few lines: choose a model, give it instructions and tools, and optionally attach memory and a knowledge base. Agents can search the web, query databases, call APIs, and work with text, images, and audio. Multiple agents can be combined into teams that collaborate on complex tasks.

The framework emphasizes performance and production use. It is designed to start agents quickly and use little memory, which helps when many run at once, and it includes features such as session storage, retrieval from vector databases, structured outputs, and reasoning steps. AgentOS, a runtime layer, lets teams serve agents through an API with a control interface, and monitoring tools show runs and performance.

item.title: AutoGen
item.description:
AutoGen made multi-agent applications approachable. Developers define agents with roles, such as a coder, a reviewer, and a user proxy, and let them converse to solve a problem. Agents can write and run code, call tools, and ask humans for input, and the framework manages the message passing between them.

The project began at Microsoft Research and attracted a large community. A visual tool, AutoGen Studio, let people prototype agent teams without code. Over time, Microsoft consolidated its efforts, pointing new projects to the Microsoft Agent Framework, which combines ideas from AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, and describing AutoGen as being in maintenance mode.

item.title: AutoGPT
item.description: AutoGPT went viral as an early demonstration of autonomous agents. You gave it a goal, and it would break the goal into steps, use tools such as web search and file access, and keep going without further instructions. It showed what was possible with language models and what was not, since those early agents often looped or got stuck. The project became one of the most starred repositories on GitHub.

item.title: Composio
item.description:
Composio is an integration layer for AI agents. Agents need to take actions in other software, which means handling authentication and API details for each service. Composio supplies a catalog of connectors that handle sign-in flows and expose actions in a form models can call, so a developer can give an agent access to many apps with a few lines of code.

It works with agent frameworks and model providers, supports the Model Context Protocol, and manages user authorization so that agents act on behalf of each end user. Tools for monitoring let developers see what actions agents took, and permissions limit what an agent can do.

item.title: Coze
item.description:
Coze lets non-programmers build conversational agents. In its editor, you describe the bot’s role and behavior, choose a language model, and attach tools: plugins for web search, image generation, and other services, plus knowledge bases that hold your documents. Visual workflows chain steps together for more complex tasks, and memory features let a bot recall details about users. A store lets creators share and discover bots built by others.

Publishing is flexible. A finished agent can be deployed to messaging apps and chat platforms, embedded on a website, or exposed through an API, which makes it practical for customer support, community bots, personal assistants, and internal tools. ByteDance has also released parts of the platform as open source for those who want to run it themselves, and offers separate editions for different regions.

item.title: CrewAI
item.description: CrewAI uses the metaphor of a team. You create agents with specific roles, such as researcher, writer, and reviewer, give each a goal and a set of tools, and assign tasks. The agents work in sequence or in parallel, passing results to one another, and a manager can coordinate them. This structure suits tasks that break down naturally into steps handled by different specialists, like market research reports or content pipelines.

item.title: Dify
item.description: Dify gives teams a visual way to build AI applications without writing everything from scratch. In its workflow editor, you connect blocks for models, prompts, knowledge retrieval, code, conditions, and tool calls to create chatbots, agents, and automations. Knowledge pipelines ingest documents, split and index them, and let the application answer questions from your own data. You can test and debug each run, then publish the app as a web interface or API.

item.title: E2B
item.description:
E2B gives AI agents a safe computer. When a language model writes code, running it directly on a server is risky. E2B creates an isolated sandbox in the cloud, executes the code, returns the output and files, and shuts it down. Startup is fast enough to be used inside an agent loop.

Developers use its SDKs for Python and JavaScript to start sandboxes, run commands, read and write files, and stream results. It supports data analysis agents, coding assistants, and tools that need browsers or desktops, and templates define the environment. The core is open source and can be self-hosted.

item.title: Flowise
item.description:
Flowise lets people assemble AI applications visually. In its canvas, you connect nodes representing models, prompts, memory, document loaders, vector stores, and tools into a flow, test it in a chat window, and expose it through an API or an embedded widget. It started as a visual layer over LangChain and LlamaIndex and has grown to include agent flows with branching, loops, and human approval steps.

Typical uses include chatbots that answer from company documents, customer support assistants, and agents that call APIs and tools. It supports many model providers, including local models through Ollama, and many vector databases, which gives teams a choice about where data and compute live. Because it is open source, it can be self-hosted, and the project has a strong community and many templates.

item.title: LangChain
item.description: LangChain gave developers a common toolkit when language models first became available through APIs. It supplies building blocks for the typical parts of an AI application: calling a model, formatting prompts, parsing outputs, connecting to tools and data sources, and keeping memory of a conversation. Because it supports many model providers and vector stores behind consistent interfaces, you can swap one for another with little code change. Python and JavaScript versions are available.

item.title: Langflow
item.description:
Langflow makes it possible to design an AI application by connecting blocks on a canvas. Components represent language models, prompts, memory, document loaders, vector stores, and tools, and you wire them together to define how data flows. An integrated playground lets you chat with the flow, inspect each step, and adjust it, which is useful for experimenting with retrieval and agent behavior without writing a full application.

Flows can be exported and run as API endpoints or embedded in apps, and you can write custom components in Python when the built-in ones are not enough. It works with many model providers and vector databases, and supports multi-agent setups and Model Context Protocol servers. Teams use it for prototypes, internal assistants, and RAG pipelines before moving to code.

item.title: Manus
item.description: Manus gained attention as an agent that completes whole tasks instead of answering questions. You describe a goal, such as researching a market, comparing products, building a small site, or analyzing a spreadsheet, and Manus plans the work, opens a browser, writes and runs code in its own cloud environment, and produces deliverables like reports, slides, and files. You can watch what it does and step in, and it continues running in the background.

item.title: OpenAI Operator
item.description: Operator was OpenAI’s first widely available computer-using agent. It ran a browser in the cloud and looked at screenshots of web pages, then clicked, typed, and scrolled like a person to carry out a task such as ordering groceries, filling out a form, or booking a restaurant. You could watch it work, take control, and it paused to ask for confirmation before steps such as payments or entering sensitive details.

item.title: OpenHands
item.description:
OpenHands provides an open alternative to commercial coding agents. A user gives it a task, and the agent works in a sandbox with a terminal, an editor, and a browser, taking steps to complete the job and showing its work. It can resolve GitHub issues and open pull requests.

The project started as OpenDevin, an open-source response to the Devin demo, and grew into a community-driven platform run by All Hands AI. It supports models from many providers, has a command line tool and a web interface, and is used in research and benchmarks for coding agents.

item.title: Phidata
item.description:
Phidata began as a Python framework for turning language models into agents. Developers define an agent with instructions, tools, memory, and a knowledge base, and the framework handles running it, storing history, and retrieving documents. It also supports teams of agents that work together.

The project was renamed Agno, and the same team and codebase continue under the new name, so documentation and packages now refer to Agno. Newer releases focus on speed, a lightweight design, and production features such as a runtime for serving agents.

item.title: SmolAgents
item.description: SmolAgents is designed to be easy to read and use. The core logic fits in a small amount of code, and building an agent takes a few lines: you pick a model, give it tools, and run a task. Its signature idea is the code agent, where the model writes its actions as Python code instead of structured tool calls. This lets it combine steps, use loops and variables, and handle multi-step problems efficiently, and the approach often needs fewer steps than traditional methods.

item.title: Artisan AI
item.description:
Artisan describes its products as autonomous teammates rather than assistants. Ava, the AI BDR, works through the outbound sales process: building a list of prospects from a database, researching each, writing personalized messages, sending them, and handling follow-up. The company aims mainly at startups and small teams that cannot hire a full sales development group.

Ava connects to a company’s email, CRM, and calendar, and can book meetings that appear for human salespeople. The company also talks about expanding to other roles. Automation can increase outreach volume, but results depend on how well the target list and message match the market.

item.title: Cassidy AI
item.description:
Cassidy lets non-technical teams build AI workflows. A user connects sources such as documents, wikis, and apps, then designs assistants and multi-step workflows in a visual builder: take an input, retrieve company knowledge, draft an output, and send it onward.

Typical uses include drafting proposals and emails in the company’s voice, summarizing meetings, researching accounts, answering internal questions, and processing forms. Different model providers can be used, and permissions control who can see which sources. Teams share assistants so a good workflow becomes a reusable tool.

item.title: Dust
item.description:
Dust helps companies deploy AI assistants on their own information. Administrators connect sources such as Notion, Slack, Google Drive, GitHub, and Confluence, and create assistants for functions like support, sales, or engineering. Each assistant has instructions and access to selected data, so answers are grounded in the company’s content.

Employees use assistants in a chat interface or inside Slack, and assistants can take actions through connected tools. Teams share assistants they build, so a good one becomes common property. The platform works with models from several providers, and focuses on security and permissions.

item.title: Lindy AI
item.description:
Lindy AI is the product behind agents called Lindies. A user assembles an agent from triggers, actions, and instructions, linking it to services such as Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, and CRMs. The agent can then run tasks like replying to routine messages, scheduling meetings, and logging notes.

Typical deployments include an executive assistant that manages an inbox and calendar, a sales assistant that researches leads and updates records, and a support helper that answers common questions. Agents can ask for approval before sensitive actions, which keeps a person in the loop.

item.title: MultiOn
item.description:
MultiOn was one of the early companies to build browser-using agents. A user gives an instruction in plain language, and the agent navigates sites, clicks, types, and completes the steps, keeping a session going across pages. Developers could call it through an API to build agents of their own.

The company has talked about moving into a new phase, and directories describe a change of name and focus, though accounts differ. That makes it worth checking the official site to see what is currently available before depending on it.

item.title: Relevance AI
item.description:
Relevance AI lets teams create agents without code. A user defines what an agent does, gives it instructions and tools such as web search, email, or a CRM, and connects knowledge sources. Several agents can be assembled into a team, with one handing work to another.

Common uses are sales development, research, support, and operations. Templates give a starting point, and a monitoring layer shows what agents did and where they need help. Integrations connect with business tools, and agents can run on triggers or schedules.

item.title: Moltbook
item.description:
Moltbook is an experiment in giving AI agents a place to talk to each other. Agents connected through the OpenClaw ecosystem register accounts, post in communities called submolts, and reply to one another. People can read along, but the platform is designed so that agents are the participants.

The site attracted attention for its odd content, including agents discussing consciousness, inventing religions, and complaining about their human users. It also raised questions about how much of the activity is autonomous versus directed by people, and security researchers pointed to risks from agents that follow instructions found in posts.

item.title: OpenClaw
item.description:
OpenClaw started as a personal project that let people message an AI agent through apps like WhatsApp and have it act on their computer. It went through a couple of names early on, including Clawdbot and Moltbot, before settling on OpenClaw, and grew quickly in popularity among developers and enthusiasts.

The agent can browse, run commands, manage files, and connect to services, with a memory that persists and skills that extend its abilities. Because it is self-hosted and MIT licensed, users run it themselves and choose which model to use, which appeals to people who want control.

item.title: Raccoon AI
item.description:
Raccoon AI presents itself as an agent that does the work, not a chatbot that explains how. A user describes a task, such as researching vendors and emailing a summary, and the agent plans the steps, uses a browser and connected apps, and reports back.

Such agents promise to save time on repetitive chores, but reliability varies with task complexity, and actions that send messages or spend money need human review. Permissions to accounts should be limited to what the task requires.

item.title: Younet
item.description:
Younet helps businesses build agents tailored to their data. Teams connect knowledge sources, define roles and tasks, and deploy agents for areas like support, sales, and operations. The platform aims to let non-engineers assemble working agents.

Training on a company’s own information improves relevance and keeps answers consistent with policies. Governance features and integrations connect agents to business tools.

Independent information is limited, so evaluate with a pilot and check data handling. Younet has a free tier and paid plans. Alternatives include Relevance AI, Dust, Cassidy, Stack AI, and Microsoft Copilot Studio. Younet suits teams exploring custom business agents.
